This modest dimension aligns with the typical body plan of small cyprinids inhabiting fast-flowing tropical waterways, where streamlined morphology facilitates efficient grazing on periphyton. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this length has been recorded at 7.1 grams [Wwi = 7.1 grams], a value consistent with the allometric scaling relationship observed across related species. Field surveys indicate that the transition to reproductive competence begins well before this asymptotic size is approached. The onset of puberty, marked by the initial differentiation of gonadal tissue, occurs when individuals reach approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters] in total length, a threshold that coordinates the onset of reproductive investment with sufficient somatic size to support gamete production. Neonatal emergence in this species begins with the fertilised egg, a demersal, yolk-laden ovum measuring roughly one millimeter in diameter. This minute wet weight at birth underscores the substantial maternal investment in fecundity over individual egg provisioning, a reproductive strategy common among small-bodied cyprinids that broadcast a large number of comparatively small, energy-poor ova. The newly emerged alevin remains entirely endotrophic during the initial days following chorion rupture, subsisting exclusively on its endogenous yolk reserves. During this lecithotrophic phase, the transparent, non-feeding larva undergoes rapid organogenesis, including the differentiation of the digestive tract and the inflation of the swim bladder, preparing for the critical transition to exogenous feeding. The depletion of yolk nutrients progresses steadily, and the point of no return is typically reached if first prey capture does not occur within a narrow window after mouth opening.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the lifespan of Paracrossochilus acerus has been documented to extend to approximately 6.5 years [am = approximately 6.5 years], a longevity figure that parallels estimates derived for the closely related model species Danio rerio. This maximum recorded longevity is relatively protracted for a cyprinid of such diminutive adult body size, suggesting that the species experiences low extrinsic mortality in its natural benthic habitat. At this temperature, the relationship between somatic growth and reproductive scheduling becomes evident: individuals channel energy into body mass increment during juvenile stages before reaching the pubertal length, after which a greater proportion of assimilated resources is directed toward gametogenesis. The longevity of approximately 2370 days [am = approximately 2370 days] under these stable thermal conditions underscores the species' capacity for sustained physiological performance over multiple breeding seasons at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C].

The specific growth trajectory from the pubertal stage to the ultimate size reveals a clear deceleration in somatic mass gain as individuals approach their asymptotic dimensions. This tenfold increase in mass from the 0.00052 gram [Wwb = 0.00052 gram] hatchling to the mature female represents a growth factor of over 13,000, a remarkable ontogenetic expansion achieved through continuous grazing on algal biofilms. The asymptotic mass of 7.1 grams [Wwi = 7.1 grams] is reached when the female attains her ultimate total length of 9.5 centimeters [Li = 9.5 centimeters], at which point somatic growth effectively plateaus and nearly all surplus energy is allocated to annual reproductive bouts. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this ultimate size is constrained by both resource availability in epilithic algal communities and by the physical limits of gill surface area for oxygen extraction in warm, frequently hypoxic tropical streams. Males follow a similar growth pattern but typically reach slightly smaller asymptotic dimensions, a sexual dimorphism common among small cyprinids where female fecundity is directly limited by abdominal volume.

Reproductive output in this species is closely tied to the attainment of the pubertal body size, with females first becoming capable of spawning once they reach a total length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters]. A typical gravid female measuring 5 centimeters will have a wet weight of approximately 1 gram [Wwp = approximately 1 gram], representing the minimum body condition necessary to support the energetic costs of oocyte development and spawning behavior. The species is iteroparous, with breeding individuals capable of producing multiple clutches over successive spawning seasons during their 6.5-year lifespan (approximately 6.5 years) [am = approximately 6.5 years] under the standard temperature regime of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This relatively extended reproductive window, combined with the production of numerous small demersal eggs, suggests a life history strategy that buffers against stochastic environmental variation in stream flow and food availability. The 7.1 gram [Wwi = 7.1 gram] ultimate wet weight of adult females thus represents the culmination of somatic growth that supports a prolonged, iteroparous reproductive output, contrasting with the semelparous strategy observed in some other small cyprinids that invest all available resources into a single, terminal spawning event.
